messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Random Neighbor GPs?
parts:
Hi folks,

In a recent thread here at stan-users, Lu Zhang posted an implementation of a Nearest Neighbor Gaussian Process, and while I am not entirely sure how it works, my impression is that it avoids computing the full NxN multivariate normal by instead cutting up the domain of the GP into pieces and a GP for each using the same kernel parameters. I'm not sure how the size/number of these pieces are chosen, and whether there is overlap between pieces; from what I can tell these choices are made outside Stan and submitted as data to Stan. 

This reminded me of a possibly silly idea I had a while ago to speed up GPs, and I'd like to know whether it makes sense and could be implemented in Stan.

Specifically, and taking the example of a 1-dimensional GP, if the data reflect N locations on the dimension, a full GP requires computation of an NxN covariance matrix and then use of this matrix as input to a multivariate normal. My alternative idea is to, for every iteration, select a random subset of size M of the N locations, where M is much smaller than N. The selection of the value of M itself could also be set to be random (uniform from 2 to N) if one wanted to avoid making the choice fixed.

I *think* this won't cause any bias in the estimation of the GP parameters, as the distribution of pairwise distances of a random subset of locations should approximate that of the full set of locations (n.b. unlike alternatives that subsample the full space with equally-spaced knots, which yields undersampling of the smaller distances). But I'm not sure whether this alters the conceptual meaning of the resulting posterior, or whether it's even possible to code it in Stan. 

On the latter, I think possibly not since the *_rng functions are only usable in the generated quantities section and presumably one can't create a model block that refers to variables defined in the generated quantities block. Another idea is to have the random sampling achieved by stepping through a matrix provided as data, but this would require the model block have access to the current iteration number, which I presume is not a feature of the language. 

Thoughts?

Mike 

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Random Neighbor GPs?
parts:
There’s a general theme with random subsampling algorithms
of this flavor.  When you subsample the data your posterior almost
never looks anything close to the full-data posterior and any samples
you generate will not be close to the typical set of the full-data
posterior, either inducing large biases when no correction is made,
or resulting in vanishing acceptance probabilities if a correction is
made.  

Perhaps more intuitively, as you aggregate more and more data
your typical set concentrates, but wiggles as it does so because
each bit of data is extremely informative and significantly impacts
the shape of the typical set.  So the various iterations of the typical
set intersect only in a few neighborhoods of very small probability.
This intuition helps explain why subsampling algorithms are so 
extremely fragile in practice.

Ten American dollars that try to subsample the input data in a GP
model will scale really poorly and we can track to back to this
intuition.

messages.author: f13fe7e880ed6103
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Random Neighbor GPs?
parts:
1) I think the simplest thing to try for scaling up the generic situations you're talking about is inducing points. (I typically work on spatiotemporal settings where Kronecker tricks are more helpful than inducing points...but combining the two is a pretty good idea!) 

I can't remember--has anyone coded inducing points up in Stan yet? The nice thing would be that you could always start with just a few inducing points as you're building/testing the model and then add some more points to see how much difference it makes. Ultimately if you can afford it at the end you could switch to a bunch of inducing points or the full thing. (Note that learning the locations of the inducing points might be hard with HMC...?)

2) I'm not as pessimistic as Mike B about subsampling working in practice. Here's a recent paper by Filippone and Engler in which they were able to get Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) to work. The main caveat from my experience with similar stuff is that tuning the parameters in stochastic gradient MCMC methods (and especially SGLD) is pretty tricky at this point. Not to mention Mike's valid concerns.

3) And finally, I just sent a simple implementation of a random Fourier features approach [Rahimi&Recht 2007/2008] to approximating GP regression to Stan-users. This uses randomization in a totally different way, and hopefully some minor improvements (see my question in that email) will make it ready for the birthday problem! 

Seth
P.S. Mike B: I'll bet you one of the new plastic fivers we have here now instead.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Random Neighbor GPs?
parts:
> On Sep 12, 2016, at 8:39 AM, Seth Flaxman <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> 1) I think the simplest thing to try for scaling up the generic situations you're talking about is inducing points. (I typically work on spatiotemporal settings where Kronecker tricks are more helpful than inducing points...but combining the two is a pretty good idea!)
>
> I can't remember--has anyone coded inducing points up in Stan yet? The nice thing would be that you could always start with just a few inducing points as you're building/testing the model and then add some more points to see how much difference it makes. Ultimately if you can afford it at the end you could switch to a bunch of inducing points or the full thing. (Note that learning the locations of the inducing points might be hard with HMC...?)
>
> 2) I'm not as pessimistic as Mike B about subsampling working in practice. Here's a recent paper by Filippone and Engler in which they were able to get Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) to work. The main caveat from my experience with similar stuff is that tuning the parameters in stochastic gradient MCMC methods (and especially SGLD) is pretty tricky at this point. Not to mention Mike's valid concerns.

I'm not sure what you're saying about "pretty tricky at this point"
but "not as pessimistic as Mike B". The latter statement's
almost vacuous in these contexts! Even I'm not as pessimistic
as Michael and I'm pretty darn pessimistic about these algorithms
working well in general without a huge effort spent tuning them
and then validating that the tuned model works.

I'm not sure why you aren't pessimistic when you say "Pretty
tricky at this point". I think that's what Michael's saying.

There's a strong publication bias and no reproducibility measured
in papers. Everyone's stochastic algorithms work in their own papers.
I haven't looked at this particular paper, but most of the SGD papers
drive me crazy because they compare a well-tuned set of learning rates
with some other algorithm. And they work on problems where they know
the right answer. One of the difficult issues with these things is
knowing when the answer you got is right. If you go the machine learning
route, that's not such a big deal, as you can concentrate on predictive
accuracy and nobody cares if you actually find the penalized MLE
or have approximated predictive uncertainty well.

My own experience has been that SGD is hard to tune even for penalized
max likelihood for logistic regression. That's why we like L-BFGS.
It tends to be much more robust.

On that point, Marcus brought up other issues of false termination
in many of the SGD algorithms when they hit a flat patch of the posterior.
This often doesn't matter if you measure held out predictions (it can even
be a good thing as it can be seen as more regularization), but
can mean that you don't actually find the optimum of the function (the penalized
MLE or ELBO optimal point or whatever). That may also be acceptable in your
applications, but be careful with it and compare to something that does
find the "right" answer if you want to claim fast general optimization.

> 3) And finally, I just sent a simple implementation of a random Fourier features approach [Rahimi&Recht 2007/2008] to approximating GP regression to Stan-users. This uses randomization in a totally different way, and hopefully some minor improvements (see my question in that email) will make it ready for the birthday problem!

Neat.

- Bob

messages.author: f13fe7e880ed6103
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Random Neighbor GPs?
parts:
These are all very good points about SGD and the related ML work on
it. What I understand Mike to be saying is that the situation is
hopeless when it comes to stochastic HMC approaches. But what I'm
predicting is that we'll eventually have ways of automatically tuning
some of these stochastic MCMC algorithms. For example, Gorham and
Mackey [https://arxiv.org/pdf/1506.03039v4.pdf] were able to choose an
appropriate step size for SGLD using Stein discrepancy.

Seth

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Random Neighbor GPs?
parts:
But what I'm
predicting is that we'll eventually have ways of automatically tuning
some of these stochastic MCMC algorithms. For example, Gorham and
Mackey [https://arxiv.org/pdf/1506.03039v4.pdf] were able to choose an
appropriate step size for SGLD using Stein discrepancy.

Lester’s work is awesome, but they are able to tune the algorithm only
under a certain set of assumptions.  Even then it’s just getting the best
performance of SGLD, which we know doesn’t scale well with dimension
and target complexity, i.e. bias that depends on the _fourth_-order 
derivatives of the target density.  Nasty stuff.

Certainly if you want to use stochastic methods you should use their
best possible implementations.  I’m just saying that that upper floor
is pretty terrible in the kinds of problems of applied interest.  As Seth
alluded, I can show this formally for HMC but the intuition carries
over to any computational algorithm.
